demand.answer:
Bottom line. Demand for licensed mobile capacity is still growing at double-digit rates. In the US it is slowing, not speeding up, and the 'AI beyond the data center' story does not yet show up in measured traffic. Since 2021 the biggest new user of US licensed capacity has been fixed wireless access (FWA): home broadband sold at a low price per gigabyte. The forecasts that show AI driving a step change are scenario models. They come mostly from equipment vendors (Ericsson, Nokia) and the carrier trade group (CTIA), and all three benefit from a spectrum-scarcity story. Revenue per GB keeps falling about 20% a year. On demand evidence alone, the thesis is plausible for 2030-2035, mainly through uplink, but the data through 2026 does not support it.

1. Growth rate and direction
US: CTIA counted 159.3 trillion MB (159.3 EB) in 2025, up 20%. That follows +38% (2022), +36% (2023) and +32% (2024). It is the slowest year since 2020 (+14%), and the 12-point drop is the sharpest slowdown in the series.

Global: Ericsson puts mobile network traffic at 203 EB/month at end-2025 including FWA (146 EB/month excluding it). Q2 2026 passed 220 EB/month, up 23% y/y, slightly faster than the ~20-21% of 2024-25, led by India and North America. Its June 2026 forecast is 515 EB/month by 2031 (17% CAGR), with yearly growth falling to 14% in 2031. The November 2026 edition is due 30 November.

Ericsson's forecasts have tended to run high:
- In 2017-18 it expected North American smartphones to average 48 GB/month in 2023. Its 2024 edition put 2023 at 26 GB. The current edition shows 21 GB for 2024 and 25 GB for 2025, with a forecast of 52 GB by 2031.
- It cut its Q3 2023 global estimate from over 140 to about 130 EB/month.
- Its 2030 forecast fell from 473 EB/month (Nov 2024 edition) to 430 (Jun 2025 edition).

Comparable mature markets settle near 20%: UK traffic grew 18% in 2025 (Ofcom), and Switzerland slowed from about 100% (2018) to 20-25% (2024).

2. FWA absorbs most new capacity
Per Ericsson, FWA was 28% of global mobile network traffic at end-2025 and rises to about 187 EB/month (about 36%) by 2031. A typical FWA line uses about 500 GB/month, against about 25 GB for a smartphone.

US subscriber bases:
- T-Mobile: 8.45M at end-2025.
- Verizon: about 5.7M at end-2025, and about 6.37M in Q3 2026 per a secondary source.
- AT&T: 2.94M fixed wireless connections in Q3 2026, including business lines.

Our cross-check: about 326M phones (54% of about 603M connections) × 25 GB × 12 months ≈ 98 EB. That leaves about 61 EB, roughly 39% of CTIA's total, for FWA and other devices. This fits about 14M average FWA lines using about 375 GB/month. Separately, analyst Dean Bubley estimated FWA made up about 90% of the 2023 increase.

So much of the US 'mobile data boom' is home broadband running on licensed spectrum. FWA growth is now slowing: Verizon added 159K in Q3 2026 versus 261K a year earlier, and New Street expected 3.6M industry adds in 2026 versus 3.8M in 2025. New Street puts Big 3 headroom at about 32M subscribers. This cuts both ways. It shows licensed spectrum can be sold as a substitute for fiber, but it also shows carriers have spare capacity today and sell it cheaply. That is not a sign of scarcity.

3. Licensed spectrum vs Wi-Fi
Opensignal found 82-89% of US smartphone data went over Wi-Fi in 2024. Many AI devices will also use unlicensed or local spectrum:
- Smart glasses connect through the phone.
- Factory and warehouse robots run on Wi-Fi or private 5G, and robot makers recommend private 5G for industrial sites.
- Counterpoint expects about 50,000 humanoid robot shipments in 2026.

Licensed wide-area spectrum matters mainly for outdoor, moving 'physical AI': robotaxis, delivery robots and drones.

4. Is AI visible in traffic?
Not in volume. Ericsson measured GenAI apps at 0.06% of mobile traffic in April 2025 (21 apps on one operator's network). Uplink was 26% of that traffic, against about 10% for mobile traffic overall. Ericsson says uplink grew faster than downlink at 43 of 55 operators, but Ookla found the uplink share flat or falling since 2023 in more than half of 22 markets.

Physical AI is still small:
- Waymo ran about 4,000 robotaxis in September 2026. At about 20 GB/day per vehicle (AT&T's network CTO), that is about 0.03 EB/yr, or about 0.02% of 2025 US traffic. Even 1M robotaxis would add about 7.3 EB/yr, about 4.6% of the 2025 total.
- Meta sold more than 7M glasses in 2025. IDC sees display-less glasses at 13.6M units in 2026 and 27.3M by 2030, and growth cooled to about 35% in Q2 2026.
- Connected-car cellular traffic grows from 1.8 EB/yr (2023) to 13.5 EB/yr (2029) per Analysys Mason, under 1% of global mobile traffic.
- T-Mobile's Starlink-based T-Satellite service was 0.0002% of T-Mobile's network usage.

The forecasts:
- Ericsson: AI could make 2031 uplink 3x (medium adoption) to 5x (high) the 2025 level. Its Technology Review models US urban uplink share rising from 10% to 14% by 2031.
- Nokia (November 2026): about 3,789 EB/month across all networks by 2035, 44% of it AI-driven. Agentic AI traffic reaches 160x its 2026 level and physical AI 105x, but uplink reaches 24% only in the cells with the most AI use.
- CTIA: about 4x US demand by 2032. That implies about 22% a year, faster than 2025's 20%.

A simple check on scale: uplink is about 10% of traffic, so tripling it adds only about 20% to total volume over six years. The stronger pro-thesis argument is physics, not volume. Handset uplink is power-limited, so uplink-heavy AI uses a disproportionate share of spectrum and favors low- and mid-band coverage.

5. Revenue per GB
Service revenue per GB fell from $412 (2010) to $4.50 (2020) and $1.48 (2025), about -20% a year since 2020. CTIA reports price per MB fell 21% in 2025, and service revenue per connection was $33.14/month versus $49.26 in 2007. Analysys Mason sees North American service revenue roughly flat to 2030. Secondary reports say the wireless CPI rose 5.9% month-on-month in August 2026 after carrier price increases; this is not verified against BLS tables. Verizon trimmed 2026 capex to $16.0-16.5B from $17.0B, and T-Mobile guided about $10B. Neither looks like an operator short of capacity.

What supports the thesis:
- Traffic still compounds at 15-20%.
- Global growth ticked up to 23% in mid-2026.
- AI traffic is uplink-heavy (26-50% uplink against 10%), and uplink is the binding constraint.
- FWA shows licensed spectrum can be sold as broadband.
- Robotaxis need wide-area coverage.

What undercuts it:
- US growth is slowing.
- Measured AI traffic is 0.06%.
- Most device data rides Wi-Fi.
- Vendor forecasts have overshot.
- The main absorber of capacity is cheap FWA.
- Revenue per GB falls about 20% a year while revenue stays flat.
- Carriers are trimming capex.
- Satellite direct-to-phone traffic is negligible so far.

6. Projections (P50, with P10-P90 range)

| Metric | 2028 | 2030 | 2035 |
|---|---|---|---|
| US traffic (EB/yr) | 250 (220-300) | 320 (255-440) | 520 (325-930) |
| Global traffic incl. FWA (EB/month) | 315 (285-360) | 420 (355-525) | 700 (500-1,100) |
| US uplink share | 11% | 12.5% | 15% |
| AI share of mobile traffic (narrow definition) | 1.5% | 4% | 15% |
| US revenue per GB | $0.98 | $0.78 | $0.52 |

CTIA's 4x-by-2032 path (about 640 EB) sits above our 2032 P90 (about 590). The AI-share ranges are very wide. Our judgment: about a 15% chance US growth goes back above 25% in any year from 2027 to 2030, and about a 15% chance AI traffic tops 10% of US mobile traffic by 2030.

Watch: Ericsson's November 2026 report, any new measured AI traffic share, CTIA's 2027 growth rate, uplink share in Ookla and Opensignal data, FWA net adds and throttling, robotaxi fleet counts, and the BLS wireless CPI.

forecast_seeds.question: How much data will US wireless networks carry per year on the CTIA Annual Survey basis (includes FWA)?
forecast_seeds.drivers_up: FWA base growing toward 25-30M lines; per-phone use 25 -> 52 GB/month (Ericsson NA forecast); higher-resolution video; uplink-heavy AI (glasses, agents, cameras) if multimodal use scales; robotaxi fleets; new mid-band capacity making FWA cheaper; satellite-terrestrial roaming.
forecast_seeds.drivers_down: FWA net adds already slowing (Verizon 159K in Q3 2026 vs 261K); fiber overbuild by the same carriers; 82-89% of smartphone data on Wi-Fi; phone base saturated; codec efficiency; carriers deprioritizing FWA to protect mobile; CTIA methodology changes.
forecast_seeds.base_rate: Mature markets settle at high-teens to ~20% growth: UK +18% (2025), Switzerland 20-25% (2024); Ericsson global CAGR 17%, slowing to 14% by 2031. US growth fell 12 points in one year. CTIA's own 4x-by-2032 path implies ~22% CAGR.

forecast_seeds.drivers_up: India and emerging-market smartphone use; FWA connections 185M -> 350M by 2031; AI uplink scenarios (3-5x uplink by 2031); 5G standalone; video.
forecast_seeds.drivers_down: History of downward revisions (2030 forecast cut from 473 to 430 between Nov 2024 and Jun 2025 editions); market maturity; Wi-Fi offload; video compression.
forecast_seeds.base_rate: Ericsson 17% CAGR 2025-2031 (515 EB/month in 2031); ABI 23% CAGR 2025-2030; Nokia 2023 report 22-25% CAGR for end-user traffic on all networks.

forecast_seeds.drivers_down: Disconnects rising with the base; same carriers prioritizing fiber; capacity pulled back for mobile/AI if demand rises; satellite broadband competition; network congestion signs (Ookla FWA speeds dipped in 2025).
forecast_seeds.base_rate: New Street: adds 3.8M (2025) -> 3.6M (2026); Big 3 capacity ~32M. Product S-curves typically flatten as 50-70% of capacity is used.

capacity.answer:
Short answer: spectrum is the cheapest way to add capacity at cell sites carriers already own, and in the 5G era it did more of the work than the long-run history suggests. But the 2025-2026 evidence does not show a binding US capacity shortage, and new mid-band supply is about to rise by statute. For licensed spectrum to become significantly more valuable per MHz-pop, US traffic growth would have to re-accelerate well above the 13-20% range it has settled into. That is not my base case.

**How capacity has been added**
The usual reading of Cooper's law splits a roughly million-fold gain since the late 1950s into three parts (arXiv 1908.06035; the factors are approximate):
- cell densification, about 1,600x;
- more spectrum, about 30x;
- better modulation and coding, 10x or less.

The 5G era looks different. From 2018 to 2025 US mobile traffic rose about 5.6x, from roughly 28.6 to 159.3 trillion MB (CTIA). Over the same period:
- Licensed sub-6 GHz spectrum in use rose about 1.6x by my estimate: C-band, 3.45 GHz, CBRS licensed blocks (PALs), 600 MHz and T-Mobile's 2.5 GHz.
- Outdoor site counts rose about 1.3x: 349,344 in CTIA's 2018 count against about 453,000 macro sites plus outdoor small cells in WIA's end-2025 count. The two counts define sites differently.
- The remaining ~2.7x came from efficiency and from running networks more heavily loaded.

A measurement study of the three US carriers found that mid-band 5G (NR) was only marginally more efficient than LTE per stream: 1.9-2.3 bit/s/Hz/stream, with T-Mobile's n41 at 3.14 because of its denser grid. The study attributed most throughput gains to wider channels. This is the strongest technical point for the thesis: in practice, wide contiguous mid-band blocks did most of the capacity work in 5G.

**Efficiency and 6G**
Within existing spectrum, 5G-Advanced adds incremental gains:
- Nokia cites 20-40% higher spectral efficiency from more antenna ports.
- Nokia also cites up to 40% more uplink capacity from eight-stream uplink.
- A T-Mobile trial of an improved multi-user MIMO method (zero-forcing) reported +60% over the legacy version.

On timing, 3GPP approved the Release 21 timeline in June 2026, with the final specification freeze (ASN.1) in March 2029. Ericsson expects the first commercial 6G systems in 2030.

6G's capacity case rests mostly on new spectrum rather than better bits per Hz:
- Ericsson's simulation says 200 MHz at 7 GHz on an existing macro grid roughly triples downlink capacity.
- Nokia's coverage modelling and a 2026 study using live-network data are less favourable: they point to denser grids and higher energy use.
- Nokia's target of 50 bps/Hz average, against about 10 for 5G, assumes extreme MIMO and 400 MHz channels. It is an ambition, not a measurement.

The candidate bands under WRC-27 agenda item 1.7 are 4.4-4.8, 7.125-8.4 and 14.8-15.35 GHz. NTIA's study of 7.125-7.4 GHz is due December 10, 2026. The 2025 budget law (OBBBA) bars auctions of 7.4-8.4 GHz and 3.1-3.45 GHz. So the 2030-2035 capacity path depends heavily on whether about 275 MHz or more at 7 GHz is cleared. That would be a supply event: it adds to the stock of licensed spectrum rather than making existing holdings scarcer.

**How credible are the shortfall claims?**
The industry studies:
- Brattle, commissioned by CTIA, projects a deficit of about 400 MHz by 2027 and about 1,400 MHz by 2032.
- GSMA says dense urban areas need 2-3 GHz of mid-band by 2035-2040.
- CTIA and Accenture (2026) say up to a third of AI traffic demand in dense areas could go unmet.

These forecasts have a poor record. The FCC's 2010 staff paper projected a deficit of about 275-300 MHz by 2014. Carriers absorbed the growth with LTE, cell splitting, Wi-Fi and later auctions, with no visible failure.

Current market data point to headroom rather than scarcity:
- US traffic growth slowed from 35% in 2023 to 32% in 2024 and 20% in 2025.
- Real prices for unlimited plans fell more than 10% in 2025, and the price per MB fell 21%.
- The combined median download speed of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile reached 334 Mbps in H1 2026, up 74% in two years (RootMetrics).
- Industry capex has been flat at about $29-30B for 2023-2025, down from $39B in 2022.
- Verizon's C-band build is about 90% complete, and its fixed-wireless (FWA) targets assume no extra capital.
- T-Mobile guides capex of about $10B, roughly 13% of service revenue. AT&T lowered its long-term capital outlook.
- Verizon's 1,741 MHz of mmWave carries little traffic: OpenSignal found capable phones on it about 0.5% of the time.

A truly scarce input does not usually see the unit price of its output fall while its buyers cut capex. Carriers do not disclose utilization; the last chart Verizon published (around 2020) said it had more unused capacity than five years earlier.

The evidence on the other side is what carriers pay:
- AT&T agreed to pay about $23B for EchoStar spectrum.
- Verizon spent $4.38B on licenses in the first nine months of 2026.
- The AWS-3 re-auction raised $3.57B, slightly above Dish's original price, with SpaceX among the winners.
- Analysts put the April 2027 upper C-band auction at $30-75B.
- The 2021 lower C-band auction raised about $81B against forecasts of $40-52B.

Prices per unit are not clearly rising, though. $30-75B for 160 MHz works out to about $0.56-1.40 per MHz-pop, against roughly $0.9 for lower C-band.

**Wi-Fi and fixed wireless**
Wi-Fi carried 82-89% of US smartphone data in 2024 (Opensignal). The US kept all 1,200 MHz at 6 GHz for unlicensed use and widened outdoor use with geofenced variable-power rules, effective April 27, 2026. The UK, by contrast, is splitting upper 6 GHz between Wi-Fi and mobile. Wi-Fi is the largest capacity lever by volume, and consumers and cable operators pay for it. Unlimited plans cut the share of time on Wi-Fi in 2017-18, and faster 5G may erode it further, but most phone use happens at home.

The counterweight is fixed wireless (FWA). It has accounted for virtually all US home broadband growth for four years and now has more than 17M connections. FWA is the main new load on licensed mid-band, but carriers choose how much of it to sell. Today's FWA sales signal spare capacity, and the ability to stop selling gives carriers a pressure valve later.

**What spectrum is worth**
The economic value of spectrum is capped by the cost of the next-cheapest capacity. The FCC's 2010 paper estimated a build using only new cell sites at $174B, against $54B with 275 MHz of new spectrum: about $120B of avoided cost. Through 2035 three forces hold down that avoided cost:
- efficiency gains that arrive with normal equipment refresh (20-40%);
- slower demand: Ericsson projects data per smartphone in North America growing 13% a year to 2031;
- rising supply: the 800 MHz statutory pipeline, 160 MHz of upper C-band, and possibly 7 GHz.

The cap is highest in dense urban cores. Traffic density there is about nine times other urban areas (GSMA), and adding sites is hardest. Spectrum and towers are complements (Peha), so a MHz is worth most to whoever owns the site grid. That points to a narrow pool of buyers, which matches the Goldman banker's view.

**Satellites and AI**
Estimates of Starlink's capacity run from 4 to 55 Mbps per km². By my estimate, a 100 MHz terrestrial mid-band layer on an urban macro grid delivers roughly 5-7 Gbps per km² (500 m site spacing, three sectors, about 5 bps/Hz). Satellites therefore cannot relieve capacity in dense areas. Satellite spectrum is valuable for coverage, and a SpaceX terrestrial play would need its own site grid.

On AI:
- Generative AI is under 1% of traffic today.
- GSMA Intelligence projects direct AI traffic at 5-20% of mobile traffic by 2030.
- Ericsson models AI tripling uplink traffic by 2031, on networks built for roughly 10:1 download-to-upload.
- Critics note that most AI agent traffic runs server-to-server, not over the radio.
- On-device inference cuts round trips, but camera and video capture add uplink.

Uplink is limited by phone transmit power as much as by MHz. Part of the fix is therefore 5G-Advanced uplink improvements and denser grids, not just more spectrum.

**Probabilities (my estimates)**
- US traffic grows faster than 20% a year over 2025-2030: about 15%.
- A visible capacity crunch by 2030, meaning per-GB price increases or capex intensity back above the 2022 peak: about 20%.
- First US commercial 6G by end-2030: about 60%.
- Upper C-band gross proceeds above $50B: about 35%.
- Licensed 7 GHz mobile service live in the US by 2032: about 40%.

**Net assessment**
Supporting the thesis:
- Mid-band spectrum is the cheapest capacity at existing sites.
- 6G capacity depends on new spectrum.
- Demand concentrates where satellites cannot help.
- Carriers and SpaceX keep buying.

Undercutting it:
- Demand growth is slowing.
- Price per MB is falling and capex is flat.
- Wi-Fi carries most smartphone data.
- Supply is rising by statute, and efficiency keeps compounding.
- Past shortage forecasts failed.

My central case for 2030 is flat to modestly higher prices per MHz-pop for contiguous mid-band TDD blocks next to the incumbents' existing holdings. I do not expect a broad re-rating of spectrum as an asset class.

Ericsson forecasts total mobile network traffic including FWA rising about 2.5x to 515 EB per month by 2031 (328 EB mobile-only); video was about 75% of mobile traffic at end-2025.
Ericsson projects North American data use per active smartphone rising from 25 GB per month in 2025 to 52 GB in 2031, a 13% CAGR.
Ericsson models that additional AI traffic could make uplink volumes roughly three times higher in 2031 than in 2025, while most networks are dimensioned for about 10:1 downlink-to-uplink.

findings.source_name: GSMA, Energy Implications of AI for mobile operators

findings.claim: An RCR Wireless analyst column argues most AI agent traffic is server-to-server WAN traffic rather than radio traffic, challenging claims that AI devices need a separate uplink capital cycle.

A common reading of Cooper's law attributes the roughly million-fold wireless capacity gain over about 60 years to densification (~1,600x), more spectrum (~30x) and communication theory (no more than ~10x).
findings.source_name: arXiv 1908.06035, PHY Research Is Sick but Curable

findings.claim: CTIA's 2019 white paper said US data carried per MHz of licensed spectrum rose 42x from 948 million MB per MHz in 2010 to 39.9 billion MB per MHz, a metric that blends efficiency, densification and loading.

The FCC's 2010 staff paper projected a spectrum deficit of about 275 MHz (roughly 300 MHz in FCC framing) by 2014 and estimated that meeting demand with cell sites alone would cost $174B versus $54B with additional spectrum.
A Brattle Group study for CTIA projects a US licensed spectrum deficit of nearly 400 MHz by 2027 and about 1,400 MHz by 2032, normalized to full-power licensed spectrum with 1-2 GHz propagation.
A 2026 CTIA report by Accenture warns up to one-third of AI traffic demand in high-density areas could go unmet within several years and calls for licensed use of the 4 GHz and 6/7 GHz bands.
findings.value: Up to 1/3 of dense-area AI demand unmet

findings.claim: GSMA's Vision 2040 study says dense urban areas will need 2-3 GHz of total mid-band spectrum by 2035-2040 (2.5-4 GHz in high-demand markets), with 2 GHz operational by 2030.
A 2021 GSMA/Coleago study estimated dense cities need on average 2 GHz of mid-band spectrum per country by 2025-2030, ranging from 1.2 GHz to 3.7 GHz across 36 cities.

The 2025 budget law restored FCC auction authority through September 30, 2034, set an 800 MHz spectrum pipeline, required at least 100 MHz of upper C-band auctioned by July 2027, and excluded 3.1-3.45 GHz and 7.4-8.4 GHz from auction.

The FCC adopted rules on July 22, 2026 to auction 160 MHz of upper C-band (3.98-4.14 GHz) as Auction 115, with bidding set to start April 27, 2027, creating a 440 MHz contiguous C-band range (3.70-4.14 GHz).
TD Cowen estimated upper C-band proceeds at $30-75 billion and FCC Chairman Carr has cited $30-60 billion, about $0.56-1.40 per MHz-pop at the analyst range (Whitesail calculation, ~335M pops).
The 2021 lower C-band auction raised roughly $81 billion in gross proceeds, well above pre-auction estimates such as New Street's $52 billion and Besen's $40 billion.
FCC Auction 113 (AWS-3 re-auction) closed in June 2026 with $3.57 billion gross bids for 200 licenses after 72 rounds; winners included AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, EchoStar and SpaceX.
WRC-27 agenda item 1.7 studies 4.4-4.8 GHz, 7.125-8.4 GHz and 14.8-15.35 GHz for possible IMT (mobile) identification, the main candidate 6G bands.

NTIA planned to release its study of the 7.125-7.4 GHz band (275 MHz) at a December 10, 2026 event, with the US position that at least that segment could support mobile use if satellite services are protected.
3GPP approved the Release 21 (first 6G specifications) timeline in June 2026 with stage 3 freeze in December 2028 and ASN.1 freeze in March 2029; Ericsson expects first commercial 6G systems in 2030.

Ericsson's simulation says adding 200 MHz of 7 GHz spectrum to an existing low/mid-band macro grid can triple downlink capacity, relying on 4x more antenna elements in the same panel size to offset propagation loss.
A 2026 study using real deployment data found that co-locating 6G upper mid-band (FR3) radios on existing sites delivers limited capacity gains at high energy cost.
Nokia's 6G white paper targets raising average spectral efficiency from about 10 bps/Hz in 5G to 50 bps/Hz using extreme MIMO and 400 MHz channels; this is a vendor target, not an ITU requirement.
Nokia says 5G-Advanced support for more antenna ports could yield about 20-40% higher spectral efficiency, and eight-stream uplink up to 40% more system capacity.

A real-world measurement study of AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon found 5G NR mid-band per-stream spectral efficiency only marginally above LTE (1.9-2.3 bit/s/Hz/stream; T-Mobile n41 3.14 due to denser deployment), with throughput gains coming mainly from wider channels.
Opensignal found 82-89% of US smartphone data traffic was carried over Wi-Fi across carriers, highest for Xfinity Mobile at 89% and 86% for AT&T users.

The FCC's January 2026 Fourth Report and Order lets geofenced variable power unlicensed devices operate in U-NII-5 and U-NII-7 of the 6 GHz band, effective April 27, 2026; the full 5.925-7.125 GHz band (1,200 MHz) remains unlicensed.
findings.value: 1,200 MHz unlicensed; GVP up to 24 dBm EIRP

findings.claim: US wireless capex per CTIA was $27.4B in 2018, peaked at $39B in 2022, fell to $30B in 2023 and $29B in 2024, and was nearly $30B in 2025, while traffic kept growing.
findings.source_name: CTIA Annual Surveys (via PR Newswire, Benton)

findings.claim: Dell'Oro expects global wireless capital intensity to approach 11% in 2029, seven percentage points below the 5G peak, and global telecom capex to fall 2% in 2026.
Verizon guided 2026 capex of $16.0-16.5B including fiber, said its C-band deployment was about 90% complete covering about 300M POPs with remaining work skewed to lower-cost small cells.
Verizon told a Bank of America conference that its FWA subscriber target assumes no incremental capital, using existing network capacity.
findings.value: Zero incremental capex for FWA target

findings.claim: Verizon spent about $4.38B on wireless license purchases in the first nine months of 2026 versus $340M a year earlier, while nine-month capex fell to $11.9B from $12.3B.
T-Mobile guided 2026 cash capex of about $10.0B against service revenue of about $76.8B, roughly 13% capital intensity on service revenue (Whitesail calculation).
findings.source_name: Quartr summary of T-Mobile Q3 2026 results

findings.claim: AT&T lowered its long-term capital investment outlook with its Q3 2026 results, with reported capital investment of $22-23B a year for 2027-28, while it had agreed to buy EchoStar spectrum for about $23B.
CTIA counted 349,344 US cell sites in 2018 and 432,469 at end-2023; WIA counted 254,850 macro sites, 198,100 outdoor small cells and 830,350 indoor small-cell nodes at end-2025.
findings.source_name: WIA, Wireless Infrastructure by the Numbers 2025

findings.claim: Opensignal data showed mmWave-capable devices connected to Verizon's mmWave network only about 0.5% of the time, although Verizon holds about 1,741 MHz of high-band spectrum.

Verizon presented charts (around 2020) saying it had more unused network capacity than five years earlier and carried about four times 2010 traffic on the same spectrum; no US carrier publishes regular utilization data.
Analyst estimates put Starlink's Ku/Ka capacity pool at about 4-55 Mbps per square kilometre, far below a terrestrial mid-band macro layer in dense cities.
US fixed wireless access passed 17 million connections in 2026, and CTIA says FWA accounted for virtually all US home broadband growth for the fourth straight year in 2025.
RootMetrics measured a combined nationwide median download speed of 334 Mbps for AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon in H1 2026, up about 74% from 192 Mbps in H1 2024.

Analyst Dean Bubley argued in Fierce that investors should question carrier assumptions on demand for exclusive high-power spectrum and that banked spectrum could become a source of risk rather than a store of value.

capacity.gaps:
1) WebFetch was blocked for nearly all hosts in this session (ericsson.com, lightreading.com, telecoms.com, techblog.comsoc.org and others failed to resolve). Every figure here therefore comes from search-result excerpts, not from reading the primary documents (Ericsson PDFs, FCC orders, CTIA PDFs, the Brattle report). supply.answer:
Bottom line. US licensed mobile spectrum is concentrated, and the 2025-2026 deals made it more so. Over the next ten years, though, supply grows faster than at any time since 2021. Low-band (under 1 GHz) is the one class where scarcity is clearly real and getting worse: there is essentially no new low-band in the pipeline. Mid-band supply is set to grow by about a third by 2030 and by roughly 60% by 2035 if the statute is followed. That cuts against the idea that licensed rights in general become "significantly more valuable." The thesis holds up best for nationwide low-band and for rights usable by both satellites and terrestrial networks. It holds up worst for generic mid-band.

1. How much spectrum exists and who holds it (Nov 2026)
- Total supply. The FCC's overall spectrum screen is 385 MHz (DA 25-919). The screen is set at roughly one-third of "suitable and available" spectrum, which implies about 1,155 MHz of sub-6 GHz licensed mobile spectrum. That splits into about 204 MHz low-band and about 1,000 MHz mid-band: AWS, PCS, WCS, 2.5 GHz, 3.45 GHz, CBRS PALs and C-band. Separately there is about 4,950 MHz of licensed mmWave, screened at 1,850 MHz.
- Concentration. As of June 2024, AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile held about 82% of screen spectrum on a MHz-POPs basis. AT&T's $23B purchase of EchoStar's 600 MHz and 3.45 GHz licenses closed July 28, 2026 and added about 50 MHz of nationwide average. That plausibly lifts the big three to about 85%.
- Holdings by carrier. TD Cowen's sub-6 GHz totals are T-Mobile 376 MHz, AT&T 314 MHz after EchoStar, and Verizon 279 MHz. PolicyTracker puts AT&T at 375 MHz on a population-weighted basis. The methods differ, so treat these as ranges.
- My split. My estimated nationwide averages are below; they are derived, not published.

| Holder | Low-band | Mid-band | mmWave |
|---|---|---|---|
| T-Mobile | ~50 | ~325 | ~600 (weak estimate) |
| AT&T | ~72 | ~250 | ~1,040 |
| Verizon | ~52 | ~235 | ~1,700 (CEO, Q3 2026) |

- SpaceX. SpaceX is now a real terrestrial holder, but most of it is not yet closed:
  - 65 MHz from EchoStar (AWS-4 40 MHz, H-block 10 MHz, unpaired AWS-3 15 MHz), approved May 12, 2026. The licenses moved into a trust on May 22, 2026, and the acquisition closing is targeted for Nov 30, 2027 (about $20B, up to $11B of it in SpaceX stock).
  - Up to 14 MHz paired of nationwide 800 MHz from Grain, signed Oct 8, 2026 at a reported ~$8B. The FCC accepted the filing Nov 10; petitions are due Dec 1.
- Smaller holders and remainders:
  - EchoStar keeps small remainders (some paired AWS-3, 700 MHz E block, CBRS PALs, mmWave) and aims to sell its remaining terrestrial spectrum by September 2028.
  - Array (former UScellular) sold to AT&T ($1.018B), Verizon ($1.0B) and T-Mobile (about $178M). It keeps its C-band.
  - Comcast and Charter hold mainly CBRS PALs (about $922M combined at auction). Comcast's 600 MHz is leased to T-Mobile, with a sale expected around 2028.

2. The aggregation rules and how much they bind
- How the screen works. It is a trigger for closer review, not a cap.
- AT&T. Its post-EchoStar holdings reach 405 MHz in some counties, including up to 110 MHz below 1 GHz, which is above the 385 MHz trigger. The deal was still approved, with conditions (faster buildout and a $2.4B EchoStar escrow).
- T-Mobile. It is attributed 328-370 MHz county by county, so it is close to the screen.
- Verizon. It sits at 242-302 MHz and has the most headroom. Its Array deal triggered enhanced review in 98 markets because of its below-1-GHz holdings, and was still approved.
- No 2025-2026 deal was blocked. The time-limited 40 MHz cap on 3.45 GHz holdings expired in January 2026.
- What changes next. The 160 MHz of upper C-band will be added to the screen after the auction, lifting the trigger to about 438 MHz. The FCC's 25 MHz auction proposal includes no bright-line limit on how much any one bidder can win. In October 2026, FCC Chairman Carr said the agency may need to look at spectrum ownership in some markets to prevent over-consolidation.
- Net effect. The rules limit the big three most in low-band and in local mid-band stacking, and they explain why the buyer pool is narrow.

3. Terrestrial pipeline
- The statute. The July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) restored FCC auction authority through Sept 30, 2034 and set an 800 MHz pipeline:
  - The FCC must auction at least 300 MHz, including at least 100 MHz of upper C-band by July 4, 2027.
  - At least 500 MHz must come from federal spectrum between 1.3 and 10.5 GHz. NTIA must identify at least 200 MHz by July 2027 for auction by July 2029, and the remainder by July 2029 for auction by July 2033.
  - The 3.1-3.45 GHz and 7.4-8.4 GHz bands are excluded (1,350 MHz in total).
- Firm:
  - Upper C-band (3.98-4.14 GHz, 160 MHz) goes up for auction as Auction 115 starting April 27, 2027, with 3,248 licenses.
  - Satellite operators estimate $4.33B to clear the band.
  - TD Cowen estimates proceeds of $30-75B.
- Done:
  - The AWS-3 reauction (Auction 113) closed June 23, 2026 at $3.57B for 200 licenses.
  - Verizon took about $3.2B of that. New Street puts the average price at $2.53 per MHz-POP.
- Likely:
  - 1675-1695 MHz plus 2020-2025 MHz (25 MHz). The NPRM came in October 2026. NTIA identified the first 5 MHz in February 2026.
  - 2.7 GHz (2.69-2.9 GHz, about 210 MHz). Federal relocation plans were approved in April 2026, and Carr targets an auction in 2028.
- Uncertain:
  - 7.125-7.4 GHz (275 MHz). NTIA's final report is due December 2026.
  - Part of 4.4-4.94 GHz. Nine Defense Department and agency relocation plans are under review.
  - 1.3-1.35 GHz, which is listed only for future study.
- Not auctions:
  - 4.9 GHz (50 MHz) is going to FirstNet through a band manager; the D.C. Circuit upheld the FCC order in July 2026.
  - NextNav's request for 15 MHz in the lower 900 MHz band is a license-modification petition. A draft NPRM went to White House review (OIRA) in March 2026, and it faces heavy opposition.
  - CBRS has no FCC proposal pending.
- My estimates of new terrestrial licensed MHz auctioned after July 2025:

| By end of | P10 | P50 | P90 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2030 | ~185 | ~395 | ~670 |
| 2035 | ~450 | ~700 | ~960 |

At P50 for 2035, that is about +60% on today's ~1,155 MHz base.

4. Satellite (MSS) bands and direct-to-device
- 2 GHz (AWS-4, 40 MHz) is going to SpaceX. In October 2026 the FCC authorized 15,000 direct-to-device satellites, with 7,500 due by Oct 7, 2032. SpaceX cannot use the EchoStar bands until the second closing step.
- Big LEO (1.6/2.4 GHz). In April 2026 (DA 26-398) the FCC dismissed petitions from SpaceX, AST, Iridium, Kepler and Sateliot to share the Big LEO, L-band and 2 GHz bands, keeping incumbents' exclusive rights. Amazon Leo's ~$11.5B purchase of Globalstar was cleared Oct 27, 2026 and is expected to close in 2027.
- L-band. AST holds rights to 40 MHz of Ligado's L-band; Inmarsat litigation continues.
- Satellite-terrestrial sharing rules. On Oct 29, 2026 the FCC proposed adding 482 MHz to the Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS) framework, which lets satellite operators use carriers' spectrum, taking it from 5 bands to 13. In April 2026 it replaced the EPFD limits (power caps that protect geostationary satellites); most of the new rules took effect July 13, 2026.
- WRC-27 (Oct 18-Nov 12, 2027). Agenda item 1.13 studies secondary MSS use inside IMT bands from 694 MHz to 2.7 GHz. Agenda item 1.7 studies IMT (mobile) identification in 4.4-4.8 GHz, 7.125-8.4 GHz and 14.8-15.35 GHz. Decisions take effect January 2029.

5. Evidence that supports the thesis
- Low-band is structurally scarce. No meaningful new low-band supply is coming.
- New buyers are paying up. Grain paid T-Mobile $2.9B plus 600 MHz licenses and agreed to resell to SpaceX about two months later for a reported ~$8B, above New Street's ~$6B view of Grain's target. AST was also reportedly interested.
- Non-traditional buyers have committed about $40B. SpaceX has about $28B across its deals and Amazon $11.5B for Globalstar.
- Satellite firms want exclusive rights. Incumbents defended exclusivity and the FCC upheld it.
- Industry demand estimates run far above supply. GSMA puts North America's 2035-2040 mid-band need at 2.7-3.8 GHz, against about 1.0 GHz of mid-band today.
- Concentration is high and the rules limit who can buy, which supports scarcity value for spectrum already held.

6. Evidence that undercuts the thesis
- Supply is rising sharply: about +395 MHz by 2030 and +700 MHz by 2035 at P50.
- Prices are not rising:
  - Auction 113 averaged $2.53/MHz-POP versus about $2.71 for paired AWS-3 in 2015, which is a real-terms decline.
  - TD Cowen's upper C-band range implies about $0.56-1.40/MHz-POP, against about $0.94 in the 2021 C-band auction.
  - AT&T-EchoStar implies about $1.37/MHz-POP and SpaceX's AWS-4/H-block deal about $1.01.
- The US mid-band "gap" is disputed. PolicyTracker counts 1-7 GHz spectrum assigned to operators at US 791 MHz, China 835, Germany 879 and UK 943 MHz. CTIA's much larger gap rests on a 3 GHz-and-up definition.
- Carriers are signaling restraint:
  - Verizon talks about "build versus buy" and says upper C-band takes 4-5 years to deploy.
  - T-Mobile says it will bid only if spectrum is cheaper than densifying its network.
  - AT&T's leverage is 3.13x and it cut 2027-28 capex guidance. Its CEO told investors not to "over-rotate" on SpaceX's single low-band carrier.
- Policy is moving toward sharing, not new monopolies: SCS leasing, the big three's satellite joint venture signed Oct 1, 2026 (pooling spectrum for satellite partners), and new auction bands that carry secondary MSS allocations. All of these make it less necessary to own spectrum outright.
- The buyer pool is narrow. Auction 113 had 17 qualified bidders and 7 winners, and Verizon spent about 89% of the money.

7. Implications by horizon
- 2028: upper C-band licensed (very likely), SpaceX closed on about 80 MHz of terrestrial spectrum (likely), and a 2.7 GHz auction underway (about 55%).
- 2030: the screen near ~500 MHz, sub-6 supply about 1,500-1,550 MHz, and the big three still above 75% of spectrum.
- 2035: the federal 500 MHz mostly auctioned if NTIA and the Defense Department deliver, with a large upper mid-band (7-8 GHz) tranche depending on WRC-27.

The scarcity premium most likely persists in low-band and in rights usable by both satellites and terrestrial networks. It most likely compresses in mid-band.

prices.answer:
Short answer: private-market prices for US spectrum went up in 2025-2026, but nearly all of the gain went to sellers, not to the shareholders of the incumbent carriers. New mid-band supply still clears at FCC auction well below the 2015 peak. The new marginal buyer is SpaceX. Whether that bid lasts is the main swing factor for 2028-2035 values.

1. What auctions have cleared at (gross proceeds; approximate $/MHz-pop; band)
- AWS-1, Auction 66 (2006): $13.7B, $0.54, mid-band.
- 700 MHz, Auction 73 (2008): $19.1B, about $1.3 on average (B block about $2.24), low-band.
- H-block, Auction 96 (2014): $1.56B, about $0.51. DISH was the only bidder and won at the reserve price.
- AWS-3, Auction 97 (2015): $44.9B, about $2.7. This is the US peak.
- 600 MHz, Auction 1000 (2017): $19.8B, about $0.93.
- mmWave, Auctions 101/102/103 (2019-20): $0.70B, $2.02B and $7.57B, all near $0.01.
- CBRS licenses, Auction 105 (2020): $4.59B, about $0.21.
- C-band, Auction 107 (2021): $81.2B. That is $0.945 on bids alone, or about $1.11 including roughly $14B of satellite clearing payments.
- 3.45 GHz, Auction 110 (2022): $22.5B, $0.70-0.74.
- 2.5 GHz, Auction 108 (2022): $0.43B, against pre-auction estimates of $1-5B.
- AWS-3 re-auction, Auction 113 (June 2026): $3.57B, an average of $2.53 per New Street. That is about 24% above an analysis of Auction 97's average, and about 4% above what DISH affiliates originally bid for the same licenses.

2. Price trend by band
- Mid-band peaked at AWS-3 in 2015. The large upper mid-band blocks then sold for less per MHz-pop (C-band $0.95, 3.45 GHz $0.74). Reasons: more MHz sold at once, shorter range, and winners paying clearing costs.
- Total dollars still rose: C-band raised more than any previous auction.
- The 2026 AWS-3 result shows that small amounts of paired lower mid-band spectrum with mature device support still fetch $2.5-3.0.
- Low-band went from about $1.3 (700 MHz, 2008) to $0.93 (600 MHz auction, 2017). It then rose in private resales:
  - 600 MHz: $2.21-2.64 (2022-23).
  - 850 MHz: $1.44 (Verizon-UScellular).
  - 800 MHz: $0.78 when Grain bought it in 2025-26, then $1.73 when SpaceX agreed to buy it in 2026.
- mmWave sits near $0.01 and is being written down. Array/TDS impaired high-band licenses, and T-Mobile handed back 24 GHz licenses.
- Globally, NERA puts the three-year average mid-band price at $0.17/MHz-pop, with 2024 a historic low. US prices are several times global levels.

3. Private deals, 2018-2026
- Straight Path (2018): Verizon topped AT&T's $1.6B agreed price with $3.1B in stock.
- 600 MHz:
  - T-Mobile paid $3.5B to Channel 51/LB License in 2022 (about $2.64).
  - T-Mobile agreed to pay up to $3.3B for Comcast's licenses in 2023 (about $2.21 if all are sold). Comcast had paid about $1.7B at auction. Only $46M has closed; the rest is targeted for the first half of 2028.
- UScellular:
  - T-Mobile bought the operations plus about 30% of the spectrum for $4.4B, including debt.
  - AT&T paid $1.018B for 3.45 GHz and 700 MHz licenses (about $0.64; closed January 2026).
  - Verizon paid $1.0B for 693M MHz-pops of 850 MHz, AWS and PCS (about $1.44; closed June 2026).
- EchoStar to AT&T: AT&T closed 30 MHz of 3.45 GHz plus 20 MHz of 600 MHz for $22.65B on July 28, 2026. That is about $1.40 blended. Per New Street it was about $9B above EchoStar's cost, and AT&T's CEO admitted the price was high.
- EchoStar to SpaceX:
  - $17B for 40 MHz of AWS-4 plus 10 MHz of H-block: half cash, half SpaceX stock, plus about $2B of EchoStar interest. MoffettNathanson puts that at about $1.03, above its own estimates of $0.75 (AWS-4) and $0.65 (H-block).
  - About $2.6B in SpaceX stock for 15 MHz of uplink-only unpaired AWS-3 (about $0.52, my calculation).
  - The licenses moved into a trust on May 22, 2026. Final closing is targeted for November 30, 2027.
- T-Mobile to Grain (800 MHz): $3.6B, made up of $2.9B cash plus $690M of 600 MHz licenses (about $0.78). It closed August 10, 2026. T-Mobile keeps 50% of Grain's later gains above Grain's invested capital, costs and a set return.

4. The Reuters 2026-10-08 deal
I could not open the Reuters page; the site blocks fetching. SpaceX's own 8-K and coverage of the Reuters story say:
- On October 8, 2026, SpaceX agreed to buy 100% of Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz portfolio: up to 14 MHz of paired low-band spectrum.
- No price was disclosed. The Wall Street Journal, cited by Reuters, reported about $8B in cash. New Street puts that at about $1.73/MHz-pop, against a rumored Grain target of $6B ($1.30).
- It needs FCC approval; petitions against it are due December 8. Closing is expected in the first half of 2027.
- Grain bought these licenses two months earlier for $3.6B, so the resale is about 2.2x total consideration, or 2.8x Grain's cash outlay. T-Mobile's 50% share of the gain means part of that markup flows back to T-Mobile.
- Musk called it the last critical piece SpaceX needed to provide complete phone coverage in America.

5. Buyers: very few
- AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile took about 96% of C-band dollars ($78.2B of $81.2B).
- In Auction 113 they took about 99%; Verizon alone took 88%. Seventeen bidders qualified, seven won, and SpaceX won $8.5M.
- Verizon and Sprint skipped the 600 MHz auction.
- Real competition appears only when a fourth party shows up:
  - Straight Path (AT&T against Verizon).
  - EchoStar, whose spectrum was split between AT&T and SpaceX. Verizon held talks about the AWS-3 licenses but signed nothing.
  - Globalstar: Amazon agreed to pay $11.57B, with SpaceX reported as a rival bidder.
- SpaceX accounts for about $27.6B, roughly 45-50%, of 2025-26 US private spectrum deal value.

6. Book values
- Carriers carry FCC licenses at historical cost:
  - AT&T: $149.4B at September 30, 2026, up from $128.1B, because of the EchoStar purchase.
  - Verizon: about $161B ($157.0B at year-end 2025).
  - T-Mobile: $100.0B.
  - Combined: about $411B.
- At late-October share prices and reported net debt, that is roughly 49%, 50% and 41% of enterprise value.
- So the market already prices spectrum at roughly book value. Higher resale prices do not reach carrier earnings unless carriers sell, which they rarely do.

What supports the thesis:
- The 800 MHz price more than doubled in two months.
- EchoStar sold at large premiums to its cost.
- Auction 113 cleared above Auction 97 even for leftover licenses.
- Amazon is paying about 40x 2026 sales for Globalstar, largely for its satellite spectrum rights.
- Anterix raised its own estimate of its 900 MHz spectrum to $2.5B-$7B+ after the FCC widened the band to 10 MHz.
- AT&T admitted it paid more than prior benchmarks.

What undercuts it:
- AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares fell 9-13% on October 9 (per NBC) when SpaceX bought the 800 MHz licenses. Spectrum in a new entrant's hands is a competitive negative for incumbents, which matches the Goldman banker's point.
- MoffettNathanson notes the three carriers still hold 14-15x as much spectrum as SpaceX.
- New supply is coming:
  - Auction 115: 160 MHz of upper C-band, bidding from April 27, 2027. TD Cowen estimates $30-75B, or about $0.57-1.42/MHz-pop, before about $16B of satellite and altimeter costs that winners also pay.
  - EchoStar's remaining licenses ($8.45B on its books) are to be sold by September 2028.
- Several bands have disappointed: mmWave, 2.5 GHz leftovers and CBRS.
- The FCC attaches conditions: an escrow and faster buildout on AT&T-EchoStar, and a refusal to let satellite coverage count toward Auction 115 buildout.
- The extra buyer is essentially one company, which now says its spectrum puzzle is complete.

Outlook (probabilistic)
- By 2028: Auction 115 will have set a fresh mid-band price. My P50 is about $42B, or about $0.80/MHz-pop on bids, below the 2025-26 private deals. A large SpaceX win would be an upside surprise.
- By 2030: low-band private prices likely hold at $1.2-2.0 (P50 about $1.6), because sub-1 GHz spectrum is scarce. Upper mid-band likely trends to $0.5-1.0 as the auction pipeline required by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act adds supply.
- By 2035: values depend on whether direct-to-phone satellite and ground networks produce more than one well-funded non-carrier buyer. If they do not, 2025-26 looks like a one-time jump driven by EchoStar's forced exit and SpaceX's build.

For passive exposure, the evidence favors owners of spectrum they have not yet sold, with few operating obligations (EchoStar's remaining portfolio, Anterix), or the buyer itself (SpaceX, reported as listed). It favors them over AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile: their spectrum is already about half of enterprise value, and their returns depend on raising prices.

findings.claim: After the SpaceX 800 MHz deal, AT&T shares fell 9.8%, Verizon 8.7% and T-Mobile 13.3% on Oct 9, 2026.
AT&T completed the purchase of EchoStar's 600 MHz and 3.45 GHz licenses on July 28, 2026 for $22,650M, carried in Licenses-Net.
The FCC approved the AT&T-EchoStar deal on May 12, 2026, requiring EchoStar to place $2.4B in escrow (tower litigation) and AT&T to build out faster than requested.
CreditSights estimated the AT&T-EchoStar price at about $1.40/MHz-pop using 325M pops; AT&T did not split the price by band.
New Street said the $23B price exceeded EchoStar's purchase cost by $9B and its securitization appraisal by $5B; AT&T CEO John Stankey said he was well aware it exceeded what Dish paid.

SpaceX agreed to buy EchoStar's 40 MHz AWS-4 and 10 MHz H-block licenses for about $17B (up to $8.5B cash and $8.5B SpaceX stock) plus about $2B of EchoStar interest; MoffettNathanson put the price at about $1.03/MHz-pop versus its $0.75 (AWS-4) and $0.65 (H-block) estimates.
EchoStar moved the licenses sold to SpaceX into Spectrum Business Trust 2025-1 on May 22, 2026; the final Spectrum Acquisition Closing to SpaceX is targeted for Nov 30, 2027.
EchoStar agreed on Nov 6, 2025 to sell its nationwide unpaired AWS-3 licenses (1695-1710 MHz, uplink only) to SpaceX for about $2.6B in SpaceX stock.
FCC Auction 113 (AWS-3 re-auction) closed with $3,572,889,200 in gross bids; 7 bidders won 200 licenses after 72 rounds, of 17 qualified bidders.
In Auction 113 Verizon won 82 licenses for about $3.16B, T-Mobile 102 licenses for $277.8M, AT&T 10 licenses for $120.8M, SpaceX two markets for $8.49M and EchoStar two licenses for $1.2M.

New Street estimated Auction 113 averaged $2.53/MHz-pop, ranging from $0.15 (American Samoa) to $5.67 (Honolulu), with Chicago above $4 and New York at $3.30; another analysis put it about 24% above Auction 97's $2.03 for comparable licenses.
Applying Auction 113's ~4% premium, New Street valued EchoStar's remaining paired AWS-3 at $8.1B ($2.94/MHz-pop); MoffettNathanson called that a floor. No buyer was confirmed.

EchoStar carried its remaining wireless spectrum licenses at about $8.45B at Sep 30, 2026 and told the FCC it would sell its 700 MHz, paired AWS-3, CBRS, C-band, MVDDS and mmWave licenses by Sept 1, 2028 if waivers are granted.
C-band Auction 107 raised $81,168,677,645 in gross bids; Verizon bid $45.45B, AT&T $23.41B and T-Mobile $9.34B; 21 bidders won all 5,684 licenses.

C-band bids equated to about $0.945/MHz-pop; winners also owed about $9.7B in accelerated relocation payments plus an estimated $3.3-5.2B in relocation costs, implying about $1.11/MHz-pop all-in (computed).
3.45 GHz Auction 110 raised $22,513,601,811 in gross bids for 100 MHz; average price about $0.736/MHz-pop.

findings.claim: AWS-3 Auction 97 (2014-15) raised about $44.9B for 65 MHz, the US mid-band price peak at roughly $2.7/MHz-pop on a paired basis.

The 600 MHz incentive auction raised $19,768,437,378 gross for 70 MHz; T-Mobile bid about $8.0B, DISH $6.2B and Comcast $1.7B, while Verizon and Sprint did not bid; analysts put it near $0.93/MHz-pop.
The 700 MHz auction (Auction 73) totaled about $19.1B; analysts put the B block near $2.24/MHz-pop and the A block near $1.17.
The AWS-1 auction (Auction 66, 2006) raised $13.7B at a net price of about $0.536/MHz-pop.
mmWave Auctions 101 (28 GHz), 102 (24 GHz) and 103 (37/39/47 GHz) raised $702.6M, $2.02B and $7.57B gross; Auction 103 was estimated at about $0.009/MHz-pop.
CBRS PAL Auction 105 raised $4,585,663,345 gross with 228 winners of 20,625 county licenses.
2.5 GHz Auction 108 raised only about $427.8M versus analyst expectations of $1-5B; T-Mobile won about $304M of it.

Array Digital Infrastructure (ex-UScellular) recorded a $47.7M impairment on retained 28/37/39 GHz licenses in Q3 2025 after an earlier $136.2M charge, citing industry-wide challenges operationalizing high-band spectrum.
Verizon outbid AT&T's agreed $1.6B deal for Straight Path's 28/39 GHz licenses, closing in Feb 2018 for about $3.1B in stock; Straight Path paid an FCC civil penalty of more than $600M.

T-Mobile agreed in 2023 to buy Comcast's 600 MHz licenses for $1.2-3.3B (New Street: $2.21/MHz-pop if all sold; Comcast paid ~$1.7B at auction); only $46M had closed by June 2, 2026, with the rest targeted for 1H 2028.
In 2022 T-Mobile agreed to pay $3.5B for 600 MHz licenses from Channel 51 License Co and LB License Co covering about 108M POPs; New Street put it at about $2.64/MHz-pop.
Verizon's $1.0B purchase of UScellular spectrum covered 663M MHz-pops of 850 MHz cellular plus 11M MHz-pops AWS and 19M MHz-pops PCS; it closed June 1, 2026.
Array (ex-UScellular) closed its sale to AT&T on Jan 13, 2026: 1,250M MHz-pops of 3.45 GHz and 331M MHz-pops of 700 MHz B/C block for about $1.018B.
Amazon agreed on Apr 14, 2026 to buy Globalstar for $90/share (about $11.57B), with SpaceX reported as a rival bidder; closing is pending FCC review and expected in 2027.
AST SpaceMobile agreed to provide about $550M to Ligado ($535M passing to Inmarsat) for long-term use of up to 45 MHz of L-band; closing still awaits FCC approval.
Anterix signed 2026 900 MHz license sales to CPS Energy (Bexar County, $13.0M, discounted), NorthWestern Energy ($7.7M), TNMP ($3.2M) and Benton PUD (~$0.8M).
After the FCC expanded the 900 MHz broadband allocation from 6 to 10 MHz (Feb 18, 2026), Anterix estimated its spectrum value at roughly $2.5B to over $7B, up from $1.5-4B.

FCC Auction 115 will offer 160 MHz of upper C-band (3.98-4.14 GHz) in eight 20 MHz blocks per PEA, with bidding starting Apr 27, 2027; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act requires at least 100 MHz auctioned by July 4, 2027.
TD Cowen estimated the upper C-band auction at $30-75B and Chairman Carr at $30-60B; the FCC declined SpaceX's request to let satellite coverage satisfy buildout.
Upper C-band winners must also fund $6.3B in satellite incentive payments ($5.6B to SES) and $3.83-5.71B of altimeter rebates, about $16B of add-on costs in total.
AT&T's Licenses-Net were $149,357M at Sep 30, 2026 versus $128,148M at Dec 31, 2025; net debt was $149.8B.

T-Mobile's spectrum licenses were $99,980M at Sep 30, 2026 versus $98,030M at Dec 31, 2025; net debt excluding tower obligations was $80.3B and 1,059M shares were outstanding.
NERA reports global spectrum prices hit a historic low in 2024, with a three-year mid-band average of $0.17/MHz-pop to end-2025, and says the long decline may have run its course.
MoffettNathanson's Julie Zhu said Starlink's mobile service is not competitive with the Big 3 and that the three carriers still hold roughly 14-15x more spectrum than SpaceX.

satellite.answer:
Summary. In November 2026, satellite direct-to-device (D2D) has a large user base but little revenue. It has already changed the US spectrum market in one specific way. SpaceX was valued at about $1.77T at its June 2026 IPO, and it is now the most aggressive buyer of terrestrial-capable spectrum in the country. That supports one part of the thesis: convergence brings new bidders with deep pockets. Two things undercut the other part. The physics says D2D cannot carry dense urban traffic. And the market reacted to each SpaceX spectrum step by selling carrier stocks. Convergence is adding a competitor and a coverage layer. It does not ease scarcity where the incumbents earn their money.

Where D2D stands. SpaceX's first-generation Direct to Cell fleet has about 650 satellites. It runs on about 5 MHz of partner spectrum (in the US, T-Mobile's PCS G block) and carries texts, some app data and limited voice. SpaceX reported about 7.4M monthly unique devices in about 30 countries at March 31, 2026. Management cited about 22M Starlink Mobile monthly users in Q3 2026, up 37% on Q2, but that metric is defined differently from the March figure. D2D revenue is not disclosed. In Q3 2026 connectivity revenue was $5.25B out of $14.6B total, so D2D is a small, unreported slice of a company whose value comes from broadband, launch and AI.

SpaceX's spectrum build:
- **EchoStar bands.** On May 12, 2026 the FCC approved the transfer of EchoStar's AWS-4 (about 40 MHz), H-block (10 MHz) and unpaired AWS-3 (15 MHz). Waivers allow terrestrial, satellite or hybrid use, and the order adds performance obligations.
- **EchoStar price and closing.** The AWS-4/H-block price is $17B: up to $8.5B in cash and $8.5B in SpaceX stock. EchoStar expects closing around November 30, 2027.
- **Grain 800 MHz.** On October 8, 2026 SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz portfolio (546 licences, up to 14 MHz). The FCC has only accepted the filing. The reported ~$8B price (WSJ) is unconfirmed. Grain bought the same licences from T-Mobile in August 2026 for $2.9B cash plus 600 MHz spectrum.
- **Why 800 MHz.** SpaceX says it needs the band because its 2 GHz holdings do not reach indoors.

SpaceX's next-generation plans:
- **Constellation.** The FCC authorized up to 15,000 next-generation D2D satellites in October 2026. Launches start in 2027, and expanded service is targeted for the end of 2027.
- **Capacity claims.** About 20x per-satellite throughput, more than 100x system capacity, and about 150 Mbps per user. These are company targets.
- **Strategy.** SpaceX partners with carriers abroad but is confrontational in the US. Shotwell said SpaceX wants to be a full mobile telco. T-Mobile said on its Q3 call it does not want to lease capacity to SpaceX. Bloomberg reported SpaceX is seeking access to at least 80,000 US cell sites; TD Cowen puts a terrestrial build above $80B.

AST SpaceMobile:
- **Fleet.** 12 BlueBirds are operating. The target of about 45 has slipped to mid-2027, and launch contracts cover more than 100 satellites over 2027-2028.
- **Financials.** Q3 2026 revenue was $42.3M, mostly gateways and government work. FY2026 guidance is $150-200M, and cash is $3.2B.
- **Service.** Intermittent nationwide US service is targeted before year-end 2026.
- **Spectrum.** Up to 45 MHz of Ligado L-band in North America (about $550M plus at least $80M a year); Inmarsat disputes these rights outside North America. Also 60 MHz of S-band priority rights bought for $64.5M.
- **Valuation.** Market cap was $24.6-37.9B in June-July 2026, against revenue guidance under $200M. Investors are paying for the option on execution.

Consolidation:
- **Amazon and Globalstar.** Amazon is buying Globalstar (about $11-11.5B; FCC approval October 27, 2026; closing in 2027). That brings about 25 MHz of MSS spectrum and the Apple relationship: Apple holds 20%, and 85% of capacity is committed to Apple.
- **Amazon Leo.** Amazon has applied for up to 5,105 D2D satellites for service around 2028.
- **Rocket Lab and Iridium.** Rocket Lab is buying Iridium at $54 a share (enterprise value about $8.0B; closing mid-2027). Iridium's NTN Direct goes commercial in Q4 2026 with Deutsche Telekom IoT.

Within about 18 months, nearly every Western satellite-spectrum asset with D2D potential has been bought or tied up by a large, vertically integrated space company.

Physics. These are Whitesail order-of-magnitude estimates, not published measurements:
- **Gen-1 D2D:** about 5-10 Mbps per beam over several hundred km2, or roughly 0.01-0.03 Mbps/km2.
- **Next-gen targets:** perhaps 1-6 Mbps/km2.
- **Terrestrial:** dense urban macro is about 1,500-9,000 Mbps/km2, small-cell layers 10,000+, and rural macro about 5-30.

A single next-gen satellite may carry hundreds of Gbps, but that is spread over a field of view of hundreds of thousands of km2. It cannot reuse spectrum as tightly as towers 0.5-2 km apart. So satellites can come within about one order of magnitude of rural terrestrial capacity, but stay about three orders below urban. That is why SpaceX itself is buying 800 MHz and looking for towers. Demand from AI devices concentrates where people and vehicles are, and that demand will be met on the ground, mostly by existing licence holders.

Regulation:
- **Repurposing satellite spectrum.** The FCC is willing to repurpose satellite spectrum for flexible terrestrial or hybrid use (the EchoStar waivers). That adds usable supply.
- **SCS framework.** It lets satellites reuse carriers' terrestrial spectrum under emission limits. Existing licences do double duty, which is the opposite of new scarcity.
- **Not checked this session:** 2026 decisions on emission limits and EPFD (satellite power limits); the EU 2 GHz MSS licence renewal (licences expire 2027); WRC-27 agenda item 1.13 on D2D in mobile bands.
- **Concentration rules.** The Goldman point holds. The buyer pool is small (SpaceX, Amazon, AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, a few intermediaries such as Grain, and AST), and the FCC spectrum screen limits concentration.

Supports the thesis:
- **Prices are rising.** SpaceX paid about $1.00/MHz-pop for AWS-4/H-block, a band EchoStar could not use for over a decade. If the $8B is right, it paid about $1.68/MHz-pop for 800 MHz that changed hands two months earlier at about $0.61 in cash (plus a 600 MHz swap).
- **Satellite assets have been repriced.** Globalstar at about $11B and Iridium at about $8B; AST pays about $80M a year for L-band.
- **Low-band is the scarce input.** SpaceX's own move into 800 MHz confirms it.
- **Coverage demand from machines is real.** Examples: the Toyota and Deutsche Telekom IoT work on NTN Direct.

Undercuts the thesis:
- **Carrier stocks fell on each SpaceX spectrum step.** After the August 2026 earnings and after the October 2026 Grain deal (one report says T-Mobile fell 7.7%; another says 13%). Markets read convergence as competition, which is the banker's point.
- **D2D cannot serve urban demand.** Its per-km2 capacity is the constraint above.
- **Revenue is small.** SpaceX does not disclose it, and AST's is mostly non-subscriber.
- **Regulators are adding supply** through flexible-use waivers and sharing.
- **Buyer demand may fade.** Once SpaceX completes about 79 MHz of owned US spectrum, its incremental appetite may fall.
- **Execution risk is high:** AST's slips, the New Glenn failure in May 2026, and Starship's cadence.

Probabilistic view (Whitesail judgment):

2028:
- About 85% that the EchoStar transfer closes by end-2027.
- Next-gen SpaceX D2D is in early deployment (P50 about 1,000-1,500 satellites).
- Starlink Mobile monthly users: P50 about 70M.
- AST: P50 about 80 satellites.
- Global D2D revenue: P50 about $2.5B.
- About 55% that SpaceX sells US retail mobile service under its own brand on its own spectrum.

2030:
- D2D satellites: P50 about 3,500.
- Revenue: P10/P50/P90 of $2B/$6B/$15B.
- About 65% that at least one more US spectrum deal above $5B is driven by a satellite operator (Ligado, remaining AWS-3, or a cable or regional holder).
- About 30% that SpaceX runs at least 30,000 active terrestrial sites.

2035:
- About 80% that D2D is a standard feature of most new phones.
- About 85% that D2D carries under 2% of developed-market mobile data.
- Revenue: P50 about $15B.
- About 20% that SpaceX is a top-four US operator by subscribers.

Investability. There is no clean passive way to own scarce spectrum through D2D:
- **ASTS** is a high-beta bet on execution.
- **SPCX** is dominated by AI, broadband and launch.
- **GSAT and IRDM** are now merger-arbitrage positions with capped upside.
- **EchoStar (SATS)** has turned its spectrum into cash plus SpaceX stock.
- **Viasat** holds contested L-band and S-band rights.
- **The US carriers** bear the competitive risk.

The evidence supports "spectrum is being repriced by new strategic buyers." It does not support "incumbent holders will capture that value through pricing."

SpaceX plans to begin launching next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites in 2027 and to offer expanded mobile service by end-2027, and intends to add terrestrial network components without giving a capex estimate.

The SpaceX purchase of EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block licences is priced at about $17 billion: up to $8.5 billion in cash and $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock valued at signing.
EchoStar's 10-K says the spectrum acquisition closing (via a trust) is expected on or about November 30, 2027.
The FCC approved EchoStar's combined spectrum sales to AT&T and SpaceX, reported at about $40 billion in total (implying about $23 billion for AT&T's 3.45 GHz and 600 MHz purchase).
SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz portfolio of 546 licences covering up to 14 MHz; the FCC has accepted the applications for filing, which is not a grant.
The Grain 800 MHz deal was reported by the Wall Street Journal at about $8 billion, but neither SpaceX nor the FCC has disclosed a price.
Grain acquired the same 800 MHz licences from T-Mobile in August 2026 for $2.9 billion in cash plus Grain's 600 MHz spectrum.

SpaceX says the 800 MHz spectrum would give Starlink Mobile the indoor coverage that its 2 GHz mid-band spectrum struggles to provide, and on October 27 asked the FCC to allow its satellites to use 800 MHz.
The FCC reportedly cleared SpaceX's acquisition of three AWS-3 licences from Tristar covering 5 MHz of uplink at 1695-1700 MHz in 62 counties.
The FCC approved SpaceX's next-generation Starlink Mobile direct-to-cell constellation of up to 15,000 satellites in October 2026.
SpaceX targets about 20x per-satellite throughput for next-generation mobile satellites versus first generation, more than 100x system capacity, and about 150 Mbps per user.
Bloomberg reported SpaceX is seeking access to at least 80,000 US cell sites, including talks with Crown Castle; TD Cowen estimated a terrestrial build would cost more than $80 billion.
Telecom shares fell after the Grain deal became public; one report says T-Mobile closed down 7.7% at $146.54, while another cited a 13% decline (not reconciled).
AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares fell after SpaceX's first earnings report detailed its plan to become a full mobile operator.
On its Q3 2026 call T-Mobile indicated it does not want to lease network capacity to SpaceX.
Light Reading noted SpaceX gave no mobile capex estimate and no operating or financial metrics for D2D in its Q2 2026 results.
Light Reading coverage of SpaceX's small-cell plan quotes an expert noting Starlink dishes are mostly rural and suburban, the opposite of mobile traffic, which concentrates in cities.
AST SpaceMobile's Q3 2026 investor slides list 12 BlueBirds (1-6 and 8-13) as unfolded and operating in orbit.
AST pushed its target of about 45 satellites in orbit to mid-2027 and says its launch agreements cover more than 100 BlueBirds over 2027-2028.
AST reported Q3 2026 revenue of $42.3 million (mainly gateways and government milestones), reaffirmed 2026 revenue guidance of $150-200 million, and held about $3.2 billion of cash.
AST targets nationwide intermittent service activation in the US before year-end 2026, has validated ground-to-space beam handovers with AT&T, and received commercial authorization in Brazil.
AST's Ligado agreement gives long-term access to up to 45 MHz of North American lower mid-band (40 MHz L-band MSS plus 1670-1675 MHz) for about $550 million plus at least $80 million a year.
Viasat's Inmarsat argues that Ligado's, and therefore AST's, L-band rights do not extend beyond North America.
AST agreed to buy 60 MHz of global S-band priority rights (1980-2010/2170-2200 MHz via EllioSat) for $64.5 million.
AST SpaceMobile's market cap was about $37.9 billion on June 11, 2026 and about $24.6 billion on July 21, 2026; a November figure was not confirmed.
AST announced a Blacklift rocket under a $1.3 billion Firefly engine agreement, with first flights planned for late 2028.

The FCC approved Amazon Leo's roughly $11.5 billion acquisition of Globalstar, which brings about 25 MHz of harmonized MSS spectrum; closing is expected in 2027.
Apple holds a 20% stake in Globalstar, committed $1.1 billion in cash to expand iPhone satellite services, and receives 85% of Globalstar's network capacity.
Amazon's application for up to 5,105 direct-to-device satellites is still under FCC review, with next-generation D2D service planned for 2028.
Rocket Lab agreed to acquire Iridium for $54 per share in cash and stock, an enterprise value of about $8.0 billion, with closing expected in mid-2027.
Iridium reported 2025 revenue of $871.7 million and operational EBITDA of $495 million (57% margin).
Iridium NTN Direct is due for commercial availability for Deutsche Telekom IoT customers in Q4 2026, after a voice-messaging demo with Toyota in September 2026.
T-Mobile's T-Satellite launched commercially in July 2025 with texting and MMS and later added data for apps such as WhatsApp, Google Maps and X.

economics.answer:
Short answer. Through November 2026, owning spectrum has not by itself produced shareholder returns for US carriers. Their stocks have moved on pricing, share shifts and perceived competitive threats. The largest spectrum-linked gains went to a seller with more than one bidder (EchoStar, about +375% in 2025), not to holders of licenses already deployed. The Goldman banker's view fits the 2024-2026 evidence, with two qualifications set out below.

1. Demand grew, but revenue did not keep pace. CTIA reports US mobile data use of 159.3 trillion MB in 2025, up 20% (slower than the prior two years). Over the same year the wireless service price index fell 4.1% and price per GB fell 21%. Light Reading, citing CTIA, puts 2025 industry service revenue at about $235B, up 69% since 2007. That is about 3% a year in nominal terms, roughly flat after inflation, over a period when traffic rose by orders of magnitude. Carriers sell capacity at falling unit prices. CTIA projects data demand to roughly quadruple by 2032, with AI-related traffic growing about three times faster than other traffic. For the thesis to work for incumbents, that demand would have to break the pattern of the last two decades. Nothing in the 2026 results shows AI devices moving service revenue yet.

2. Q3 2026: growth came from taking share, not from raising prices. Verizon added 406k postpaid phones (44k a year earlier), its best third quarter in five years, and raised 2026 guidance to 1.1-1.2M. But postpaid ARPA fell 1.9% to $168.08, so the growth was bought with promotions and lower prices. CEO Dan Schulman has said the earlier price-led strategy cost about 2.25M net adds, and he pledged no increases "without corresponding value." Verizon still raised its top plan $5 for new customers in May 2026. AT&T added 379k (405k a year earlier), held churn at 0.92%, and grew wireless service revenue 5.0% to $17.8B. T-Mobile stopped disclosing phone net adds. Its postpaid account adds fell 31% to 274k and account churn rose 12 bps to 1.09%. Still, its ARPA rose 4% to $155.73 and postpaid service revenue rose 9%. T-Mobile is the one carrier showing pricing power.

Cable keeps taking share. Charter added 508k mobile lines pro forma (13.5M total, including Cox) and Comcast added 368k (about 10.6M). The two cable companies' roughly 876k lines exceeded AT&T's and Verizon's combined phone adds (785k). About half of Comcast's postpaid connects were free lines. This is a promotional market, not one where scarce spectrum lets carriers raise prices.

3. Returns came from lower capex and higher free cash flow. After the 5G peak, industry network investment was about $30B in 2025 (CTIA). Verizon guides 2026 capex to $16.0-16.5B. T-Mobile expects about $10.0B, and its Q3 cash capex was down 14%. Charter's Q3 capex fell 11.2%. Free cash flow rose: T-Mobile guides adjusted FCF of $18.7-18.8B, and AT&T generated $5.0B in Q3. Shareholder value in this sector is mostly dividends and buybacks funded by FCF (Verizon yields about 6.1%). Spectrum shows up mainly as a cost to be recovered: AT&T paid $23B for EchoStar's 50 MHz, a deal that closed on July 28, 2026.

4. Market structure after EchoStar. The FCC approved EchoStar's sales on May 12, 2026, with a $2.4B escrow condition. The US went from four facilities-based carriers to three, and Boost now runs as a hybrid MVNO on AT&T. Alongside the three carriers are cable MVNOs with about 24M lines and SpaceX as a growing spectrum holder. SpaceX is buying AWS-4/H-block spectrum from EchoStar for about $17B, with closing reportedly expected around late 2027. It is also buying up to 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz spectrum from Grain Management, reportedly for about $8B and pending FCC approval. The FCC has approved 15,000 Gen2 satellites. Normally a move from four networks to three supports pricing. Here cable, and the prospect of SpaceX, have offset that.

5. SpaceX is a credible bidder, an unproven operator, and a large factor in carrier stock prices. In its favor:
- Q2 2026 revenue of $7.8B, about double a year earlier
- 12M Starlink subscribers and 7.4M monthly unique direct-to-cell devices
- public stock it can use to pay for deals
- a stated intent to compete with the major US carriers
- reported talks to use about 80,000 cell sites

Against it:
- Satellites have limited capacity indoors and in dense areas. T-Mobile says more than 70% of traffic is indoors.
- Its key spectrum deals have not closed.
- Starlink ARPU fell 22%, and the company still posts losses.
- T-Mobile has ruled out an MVNO deal.

DISH is the reference case: an entrant with plenty of spectrum that never scaled, and that captured value by selling its licenses.

The market treats SpaceX's spectrum purchases as bad for incumbents. Carriers fell 4-5% on the September 2025 EchoStar deal, and 2-4% after hours when SpaceX outlined its mobile plans in August 2026. On October 9, 2026 they fell 9.8% (AT&T), 8.8% (Verizon) and 13.3% (T-Mobile, its worst day as a public company). That is the opposite of what the thesis predicts for license holders. Verizon was still up about 14% for 2026 by mid-November, while T-Mobile was down about 22% by late October.

6. Valuation. Our own estimates, which are not sourced and carry low confidence, put EV/EBITDA at about 6.5-7.5x and license book value at about 38-47% of enterprise value. At those multiples, the market pays no premium for spectrum over what the carriers paid for it. The value is real but hard to unlock: turning it into cash means selling to a small, regulated set of buyers or raising prices.

7. Scoring the banker's view.
- "Buyers are not broad and control is regulated": supported. In 2025-26 the buyers were AT&T, SpaceX, Grain (an intermediary) and a few smaller in-market deals, all under FCC conditions.
- "Telcos see no value unless they can raise prices": supported for Verizon (ARPA down 1.9%, its price-hike strategy reversed) and for the industry (service price index down 4.1%). T-Mobile is the exception, with ARPA up 4%.
- "Competition goes the other way": supported by cable's adds, free-line promotions, T-Mobile's higher churn and the stock reactions to SpaceX.

Two qualifications:
- License holders can capture value when an outside bidder appears. EchoStar went from near-bankruptcy to the best shareholder return in the Fortune 500. The 800 MHz licenses reportedly moved from T-Mobile to Grain to SpaceX for about $8B, roughly $1.7 per MHz-pop if 14 MHz is the total width. So incumbents can sell non-core licenses at a premium.
- Fewer networks, plus SpaceX's need for land-based infrastructure, create options for wholesale deals, tower leases or M&A. MoffettNathanson argued T-Mobile could benefit, and Morgan Stanley called the Grain deal constructive for tower companies.

8. Probabilistic view (our judgment). For 2030 we weight three states:
- Grind (about 50%): service revenue grows 2-3% a year to roughly $255-270B, multiples stay at 6-7.5x, cable reaches 33-37M lines, and SpaceX has fewer than 3M direct US subscribers.
- Price pressure (about 30%): SpaceX and cable push ARPA down, service revenue is flat in nominal terms, and multiples fall to 5-6x.
- Convergence premium (about 20%): spectrum scarcity is turned into cash through sales or M&A (for example, SpaceX or a hyperscaler buys a carrier or a large spectrum block), and incumbents re-rate to 8x or more.

For 2028 the ranges are narrower and the grind case is more likely (about 60%), because the SpaceX deals close in 2027 at the earliest and building a network takes years. By 2035 the ranges are wide. A 6G and upper C-band capex cycle starting around 2030 would weigh on free cash flow in every state.

For a passive investor, the evidence says AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile are cash-flow and dividend holdings with spectrum carried at cost, not a way to own rising spectrum value. Exposure to that theme has come through sellers in contested sales and possibly tower companies, and those gains were event-driven and volatile. AST SpaceMobile, for example, rose 244% in 2025 and was down about 55% in 2026 by mid-November.
